question: The Spanish Government has approved the draft Code of Criminal Procedures, which makes criminal investigations the responsibility of the Ministry of Justice – whose attorney general is appointed by the Executive – and limits the recourse to popular accusation.

Various judicial and prosecutorial associations have warned that this reform could compromise legal independence, the separation of powers, and effective remedy enshrined in Articles 2 and 19 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU) and Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union.

The Commission’s rule of law report recommended that Spain strengthen the Ministry of Justice’s autonomy and make the fight against corruption more effective. However, this reform could instead weaken mechanisms for investigating crimes that impact the EU’s financial interests and corruption. 1.
Does the Commission consider this reform to be compatible with the values of the rule of law and legal independence, as provided for in Articles 2 and 19 of the TEU?
Will the Commission assess this legislation in the next rule of law report and will it first initiate a dedicated dialogue with the Spanish Government for it to be withdrawn?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.1.2026) The 2025 Rule of Law Report1 recommended that Spain should strengthen efforts to address the challenges related to the length of investigations and prosecutions to increase the efficiency in handling high-level corruption cases, including by finalising the reform of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

Second, Spain should strengthen the statute of the Prosecutor General, in particular regarding the separation of the terms of office of the Prosecutor General from that of the Government, taking into account European standards on independence and autonomy of the prosecution and acknowledge that while the then draft law regarding ‘accion popular’ stated objective, considering a ruling of the Supreme Court, was to prevent perceived abuses of this mechanism, some stakeholders had criticised the planned reform, considering its envisaged limitations excessive and undermining in practice the value of this mechanism.

The Commission monitors carefully the implementation of all recommendations included in the 2025 Rule of Law Report and continues following national developments, including in Spain, and engaging with the national authorities and relevant stakeholders in this respect. The Commission’s assessment of steps taken to meet the recommendations will be set out in the next edition of the Rule of law Report in 2026.
